Paul Mccrorie <Paul.McCrorie@glasgow.ac.uk>:
Hi Amin Thanks for getting back to us. We recognise you have some information about accuracy in your metadata, however, the accompanying description isn't very informative about how you reach your accuracy outcome. With our own GPS receivers we have been using elements of the Dilution of Precision construct, which helps us look at how the geometry of the satellites affects the accuracy of position. We also use the signal to noise ratio to make judgement calls on things think indoor/outdoor classification. We recognise the data collected by Avicenna comes from multiple providers, as per your metadata. So certain accuracy metrics might only be relevant to specific providers. But having some indication about how your 'accuracy' variable is calculated across these would be valuable. Thanks Paul

Mohammad Hashemian <product@avicennaresearch.com>:
Good morning Paul.My name is Mohammad from Avicenna and I think I can better answer this question.We collect GPS data using Android and Apple's standard API. We store the metadata they provide along with each data point. None of the meatdata you see is calculated by us directly (I'll talk about our post-processing below). The metadata are received directly from API. And to understand what they mean and how they are calculated, the best is to check the documentation from Apple and Google. For example, here you can find the documentation from Google on Accuracy:https://developer.android.com/reference/android/location/Location#getAccuracy()If you want to know how to interpret the location record, first you should check the device_id field. This field determines the device recorded the GPS. It's either iOS, Android, or wearable (WIP). As a rule of thumb, 32-character IDs are for iOS and 16-character IDs are for Android (the exact device is stored under the `devices` table and can be exported from the Participation page of the online dashboard).Now if iOS, there is a good level of homogeneity across devices. But in Android you may want to consider manufacturer and model as well (e.g. Xiaumi v.s Samsung vs. Pixel etc.)Android also provides a metadata called "provider" (details here: https://developer.android.com/reference/android/location/LocationProvider). I think you were referring to this provider in your email. I wrote this to make sure we are on the same page that provider (to the best of my knowledge) is only defined for Android locations. If you have any questions or clarifications, please let me know.Best, Mohammad--Avicenna Research (formerly Ethica Data)4109 - 295 Adelaide St W, Toronto, ON M5V 0L4, Canada Email: product@avicennaresearch.com - Web: https://avicennaresearch.com-- On Monday, September 30, 2024 at 4:20:51 AM,

Fiona Caryl <Fiona.Caryl@glasgow.ac.uk>:
Hi Mohammad, The location#getAccuracy you linked to for Android states the accuracy refers to “the estimated horizontal accuracy radius in meters of [the] location at the 68th percentile confidence level.” Hence, if a location has an accu=10m this means a 68% chance (or 1 SD assuming a normal distribution of error) the true location is within this distance from the give location (and 95% chance it is within 19.6 m i.e. 1.96 SD). Q1: Do you know if the same is the case for iOS? E.g., do their accu values correspond to certainty of 1 SD (68%)? The SNR is a valuable metric for classifying location outdoors/indoors. It would be good if each location was attributed a SNR value. This SO post seems to have achieved this for Android https://stackoverflow.com/a/50927122 Q2: Is SNR something you can pull out from post-processing for both Android and iOS? Best wishes, Fiona
----
